title: Watch water resistance explained: what 5 ATM and 10 ATM really mean
metaDescription: What ATM and metre water resistance ratings mean on smartwatches and fitness trackers, which are safe for swimming, and what damages the seals.
excerpt: A watch rated to 50 metres is not meant for diving to 50 metres. Here is what the ratings mean and which activities each one covers.
_note: AI-assisted draft from public sources. Check every fact, add your own experience and photos, then publish from /studio.
answer: ATM ratings describe the pressure a watch withstood in a static test, not a safe diving depth. 5 ATM (50 metres) is generally fine for swimming in a pool or the sea. 10 ATM (100 metres) adds margin for snorkelling and water sports. Neither covers scuba diving unless the watch is specifically certified as a dive watch, and hot water and soap are hazards for any watch.

sections.heading: Two rating systems
sections.body:
Smartwatches and fitness trackers use two kinds of water rating:

- **IP ratings** (such as IP68) from IEC 60529, the same as phones. They describe resistance to dust and water immersion under the maker's test conditions, but are not designed for swimming.
- **ATM ratings** (such as 5 ATM) or a depth in metres, based on the international standard for water-resistant watches, ISO 22810. One ATM is roughly the pressure of the atmosphere at sea level; each additional ATM is about 10 metres of still water.

Many watches carry both: an ATM rating for swimming and an IP rating for dust.

sections.heading: Why 50 metres does not mean 50 metres
sections.body: The ratings come from static pressure tests, with the watch held still in a chamber. Movement in water creates bursts of higher pressure. Diving in, swimming fast strokes or jumping from a board generate pressure spikes well above the still-water figure for the depth you are at. That is why a watch rated to 30 metres is not recommended for swimming at all, and 50 metres is the usual minimum.

sections.heading: What each rating is good for
sections.body:
- **IP67/IP68 only, or 3 ATM (30 metres):** rain, hand washing, splashes. Not for swimming.
- **5 ATM (50 metres):** swimming in a pool or the sea, showering in cool water. The most common rating on fitness watches with swim tracking.
- **10 ATM (100 metres):** swimming, snorkelling and surface water sports with more margin.
- **Dive rated (ISO 6425, or EN13319 for dive computers):** scuba diving. Only watches specifically certified for diving should be used underwater beyond snorkelling depth.

sections.heading: What damages the seals
sections.body:
- **Hot water** in saunas, hot tubs and hot showers makes materials expand and can let steam in.
- **Soap, shampoo and sun cream** can degrade seals and the water-repellent coatings around speaker and microphone holes.
- **Salt and chlorine** leave deposits; rinse the watch in fresh water afterwards.
- **Impacts and age.** Drops and years of wear weaken seals. Water resistance is not permanent.
- **Pressing buttons underwater** on watches not designed for it can let water past the button seal.

sections.heading: Looking after a water-resistant watch
sections.body:
- Rinse in fresh water after the sea or pool and dry it, including under the strap.
- Use the water lock or swim mode if your watch has one; it prevents accidental touches and can eject water from the speaker afterwards.
- Avoid charging until the charging contacts are dry.
- Check the warranty, as many exclude water damage despite the rating.

For swimming, look for a watch with dedicated pool and open water modes, which count lengths and track strokes using motion sensors.

faq.q: Can I swim with a 5 ATM watch?
faq.a: Yes. 5 ATM is generally rated for swimming in a pool or the sea, but not for diving, high-speed water sports or hot tubs.

faq.q: Is IP68 the same as waterproof for swimming?
faq.a: No. IP68 tests still-water immersion and is not designed for the pressure changes of swimming. Look for a 5 ATM rating or higher for swimming.
